q: Statements: All pens are books. All books are papers. Conclusions: I. All pens are papers. II. Some papers are books.
exp: From All pens are books and All books are papers, all pens are papers. Also, All books are papers implies some papers are books. Hence both follow.

q: Statements: All cats are animals. Some animals are dogs. Conclusions: I. Some cats are dogs. II. Some animals are cats.
exp: Some animals being dogs does not establish any relation between cats and dogs. Also, All cats are animals does not necessarily establish existence of cats. Hence neither follows.

q: Statements: Some books are pens. All pens are blue. Conclusions: I. Some books are blue. II. All blue things are pens.
exp: The books that are pens must be blue, so some books are blue. The reverse statement that all blue things are pens is not given. Hence only I follows.

q: Statements: No flowers are fruits. Some roses are flowers. Conclusions: I. Some roses are not fruits. II. No roses are fruits.
exp: The roses that are flowers cannot be fruits, so some roses are not fruits. But we cannot say all roses are flowers. Hence only I follows.

q: Statements: All cars are vehicles. No vehicles are bicycles. Conclusions: I. No cars are bicycles. II. Some vehicles are not bicycles.
exp: Since all cars are vehicles and no vehicles are bicycles, no cars can be bicycles. But existence of vehicles is not established, so II does not necessarily follow under strict logic.

q: Statements: Some teachers are writers. All writers are readers. Conclusions: I. Some teachers are readers. II. Some readers are teachers.
exp: The teachers who are writers must be readers. Thus some teachers are readers, and equivalently some readers are teachers.

q: Statements: No apples are oranges. Some fruits are apples. Conclusions: I. Some fruits are not oranges. II. Some fruits are oranges.
exp: Some fruits are apples, and no apples are oranges. Therefore those fruits are not oranges. There is no basis for some fruits being oranges.

q: Statements: All doctors are educated. Some educated people are athletes. Conclusions: I. Some doctors are athletes. II. Some athletes are educated.
exp: Some educated people are athletes directly gives some athletes are educated. It does not establish that any doctors are athletes.

q: Statements: Some chairs are tables. No tables are desks. Conclusions: I. Some chairs are not desks. II. Some chairs are desks.
exp: The chairs that are tables cannot be desks. Therefore some chairs are not desks. The second conclusion does not follow.

q: Statements: All birds are animals. No animals are plants. Conclusions: I. No birds are plants. II. Some animals are birds.
exp: Birds are contained within animals, and animals are disjoint from plants. Hence no birds are plants. Existence of birds is not established, so II does not necessarily follow.

q: Statements: Some A are B. Some B are C. Conclusions: I. Some A are C. II. Some C are B.
exp: Some B are C directly gives some C are B. The two 'some' groups involving B need not overlap, so some A are C does not follow.

q: Statements: All M are N. No N are P. Conclusions: I. No M are P. II. Some P are not M.
exp: Since M is a subset of N and N is disjoint from P, M is also disjoint from P. II requires existence of P, which is not given.

q: Statements: Some engineers are managers. No managers are doctors. Conclusions: I. Some engineers are not doctors. II. Some engineers are doctors.
exp: The engineers who are managers cannot be doctors. Thus some engineers are not doctors. No engineer doctor relationship is otherwise established.

q: Statements: All roses are flowers. Some flowers are red. Conclusions: I. Some roses are red. II. Some red things are flowers.
exp: Some flowers are red means some red things are flowers. But those red flowers need not be roses. Hence only II follows.

q: Statements: No laptops are tablets. Some tablets are devices. Conclusions: I. Some devices are not laptops. II. Some laptops are devices.
exp: The tablets that are devices cannot be laptops. Hence some devices are not laptops. There is no evidence that any laptops are devices.

q: Statements: All singers are artists. Some artists are dancers. Conclusions: I. Some singers are dancers. II. Some dancers are artists.
exp: Some artists are dancers directly gives some dancers are artists. It does not imply that singers are among those dancers.

q: Statements: Some books are novels. No novels are magazines. Conclusions: I. Some books are not magazines. II. No books are magazines.
exp: The books that are novels cannot be magazines, so some books are not magazines. Other books may be magazines, so II does not follow.

q: Statements: All trains are vehicles. Some vehicles are electric. Conclusions: I. Some trains are electric. II. Some electric things are vehicles.
exp: Some vehicles are electric is equivalent to some electric things being vehicles. It does not imply that any trains are electric.

q: Statements: No students are teachers. Some students are athletes. Conclusions: I. Some athletes are not teachers. II. No athletes are teachers.
exp: The student-athletes cannot be teachers, so some athletes are not teachers. Other athletes may be teachers, so II does not follow.

q: Statements: All P are Q. Some Q are R. Conclusions: I. Some P are R. II. Some R are Q.
exp: Some Q are R directly gives some R are Q. The P elements need not be among the Q-R overlap.

q: Statements: Some lawyers are writers. All writers are graduates. Conclusions: I. Some lawyers are graduates. II. Some graduates are lawyers.
exp: The lawyers who are writers must be graduates. Hence some lawyers are graduates and some graduates are lawyers.

q: Statements: No A are B. Some C are A. Conclusions: I. Some C are not B. II. Some C are B.
exp: The C elements that are A cannot be B. Therefore some C are not B. No C-B overlap is implied.

q: Statements: All books are useful. Some useful things are expensive. Conclusions: I. Some books are expensive. II. Some expensive things are useful.
exp: Some useful things are expensive directly means some expensive things are useful. It does not mean those expensive things are books.

q: Statements: Some doctors are teachers. No teachers are engineers. Conclusions: I. Some doctors are not engineers. II. No doctors are engineers.
exp: The doctor-teachers cannot be engineers, so some doctors are not engineers. Other doctors may still be engineers.

q: Statements: All fruits are healthy. No healthy things are harmful. Conclusions: I. No fruits are harmful. II. Some healthy things are fruits.
exp: Since fruits are healthy and healthy things are not harmful, fruits cannot be harmful. Existence of fruits is not necessarily given.

q: Statements: Some A are B. No B are C. Conclusions: I. Some A are not C. II. Some C are not A.
exp: The A-B elements cannot be C, so some A are not C. No existence of C outside A is established.

q: Statements: All pens are stationery. Some stationery are costly. Conclusions: I. Some pens are costly. II. Some costly things are stationery.
exp: Some stationery are costly directly gives some costly things are stationery. The costly stationery need not be pens.

q: Statements: No cats are dogs. Some animals are cats. Conclusions: I. Some animals are not dogs. II. Some animals are dogs.
exp: The animals that are cats cannot be dogs. Hence some animals are not dogs. The second conclusion is not established.

q: Statements: All managers are graduates. Some managers are employees. Conclusions: I. Some employees are graduates. II. All employees are graduates.
exp: The employees who are managers must be graduates. But not all employees need be managers, so II does not follow.

q: Statements: Some cars are red. All red things are attractive. Conclusions: I. Some cars are attractive. II. Some attractive things are cars.
exp: The red cars are attractive, so some cars are attractive. These same objects also show that some attractive things are cars.

q: Statements: No teachers are doctors. All doctors are graduates. Conclusions: I. No teachers are graduates. II. Some graduates are not teachers.
exp: Doctors are graduates, but graduates can exist independently of doctors. Neither conclusion is guaranteed from the given statements.

q: Statements: Some books are old. Some old things are valuable. Conclusions: I. Some books are valuable. II. Some valuable things are old.
exp: Some old things are valuable directly gives some valuable things are old. The old books need not be among the valuable old things.

q: Statements: All A are B. No B are C. Some D are A. Conclusions: I. Some D are not C. II. Some D are B.
exp: Some D are A, and all A are B, so some D are B. Since B and C are disjoint, those D are also not C. Hence both follow.

q: Statements: Some flowers are red. All red things are beautiful. No beautiful things are ugly. Conclusions: I. Some flowers are beautiful. II. Some flowers are not ugly.
exp: The red flowers are beautiful and beautiful things are not ugly. Therefore some flowers are beautiful and some flowers are not ugly.

q: Statements: All A are B. All B are C. No C are D. Conclusions: I. No A are D. II. Some B are not D.
exp: A is contained in B, B in C, and C is disjoint from D. Therefore A is disjoint from D. Existence of B is not established for II.

q: Statements: Some X are Y. All Y are Z. No Z are W. Conclusions: I. Some X are Z. II. Some X are not W.
exp: The X-Y elements are Z because all Y are Z, so some X are Z. Since no Z are W, those X are also not W. Both follow.

q: Statements: All A are B. Some B are C. No C are D. Conclusions: I. Some B are not D. II. Some A are not D.
exp: The B-C elements cannot be D, so some B are not D. Nothing guarantees any A lies in the C group.

q: Statements: Some P are Q. All Q are R. Some R are S. Conclusions: I. Some P are S. II. Some S are Q.
exp: The P-Q group lies within R, while the R-S group may be different. Neither overlap is guaranteed.

q: Statements: All books are papers. Some papers are files. Conclusions: I. Some books are files. II. Some files are papers.
exp: Some papers are files directly means some files are papers. It does not imply that books are among those files.

q: Statements: No A are B. Some C are B. Conclusions: I. Some C are not A. II. No C are A.
exp: The C-B elements cannot be A, so some C are not A. But other C elements may be A.

q: Statements: All students are learners. Some learners are readers. Conclusions: I. Some students are readers. II. Some readers are learners.
exp: Some learners are readers directly gives some readers are learners. The readers need not be students.

q: Statements: Some A are B. Some B are C. No A are C. Conclusions: I. The two groups of B are necessarily different. II. Some B are not A.
exp: Since no A are C, the B elements that are A cannot be the B elements that are C. Also, the B-C elements are not A, so some B are not A. Thus only II follows.

q: Statements: All A are B. Some B are C. Can some A be C?
exp: A is only constrained to lie within B. Some B are C, so it is possible for some A to overlap C, though not necessary.

q: Statements: No A are B. Some C are A. Can some C be B?
exp: The C elements that are A cannot be B because no A are B. Therefore some C being both A and B is impossible for those elements.

q: Statements: All doctors are educated. Some educated people are artists. Can some doctors be artists?
opts: Only if all artists are doctors
exp: Doctors are a subset of educated people. Since some educated people are artists, the artist group can overlap with doctors without violating any statement. Hence it is possible.

q: Statements: No engineers are musicians. Some artists are musicians. Can some artists be engineers?
exp: The artists who are musicians cannot be engineers. However, non-musician artists could be engineers. Hence it is possible.

q: Statements: All P are Q. No Q are R. Can some P be R?
opts: Only if some Q are R
exp: Since every P is Q and no Q is R, no P can be R. Hence the possibility is impossible.

q: Statements: Some books are pens. Some pens are expensive. Can some books be expensive?
opts: Only if all pens are books
exp: The books that are pens and the expensive pens may overlap. Nothing prevents some books from being expensive, so it is possible but not definite.

q: Statements: All A are B. No B are C. Some D are C. Conclusions: I. Some D are not B. II. Some D are not A.
exp: The D-C elements cannot be B, so some D are not B. Since all A are B, anything not B cannot be A. Hence some D are not A as well.

q: Statements: Some X are Y. No Y are Z. Conclusions: I. Some X are not Z. II. No X are Z.
exp: The X-Y elements cannot be Z, so some X are not Z. Other X elements may be Z, so II does not follow.

q: Statements: All M are N. Some M are P. No P are Q. Conclusions: I. Some N are not Q. II. Some M are not Q.
exp: Some M are P, and no P are Q, so those M are not Q. Since all M are N, those same elements are N and not Q. Both conclusions follow.

q: Statements: Some teachers are poets. All poets are creative. No creative people are dull. Conclusions: I. Some teachers are creative. II. Some teachers are not dull.
exp: The teacher-poets are creative, and no creative people are dull. Hence some teachers are creative and some teachers are not dull.

q: Statements: All A are B. Some B are C. No C are D. Which conclusion is definitely true?
exp: The B-C elements cannot be D, so some B are not D. Nothing establishes overlap between A and C.

q: Statements: Some cars are vehicles. All vehicles are machines. Conclusions: I. Some cars are machines. II. Some machines are cars.
exp: The cars that are vehicles must be machines. Thus some cars are machines, and those same objects are machines that are cars.

q: Statements: No teachers are students. Some graduates are teachers. Conclusions: I. Some graduates are not students. II. Some graduates are students.
exp: The graduate-teachers cannot be students, so some graduates are not students. The second conclusion is unsupported.

q: Statements: All A are B. Some B are C. Conclusions: I. Some A can be C. II. No A can be C.
exp: There is no restriction between A and C. Since A is within B and some B are C, A may overlap C. Therefore I is possible, while II is not necessarily true.
